Everybody who has ever been to the coast of these islands has become aware that changes in the outline of the land are continually taking place. In some parts of the east coast of England, such as that which lies between Harwich and Walton-on-the-Naze, the sea appears to be slowly encroaching on the land, so that places which were grazing-fields twenty or thirty years ago are now covered by the sea at high tide, and at low tide are mere sandy wastes threaded by rivulets of sea-water. On the south coast of the Isle of Wight, between Sandown and the Culver Cliff, which is the most easterly point, the same loss of land is going on in another way. Some years ago a fort stood rather near the edge of the cliff, and it would have been possible to climb round the seaward wall of the fort. It is not possible now, for the outer sea-wall of the fort has long ago slipped into the sea; so have some of the inner fortifications: and it has been necessary to dismantle the whole of this fort lest every part of even the inner landward wall should follow the outer parts and slip with the solid ground down the cliff. It is easy to see what is happening here. The wind and the waves are undermining and honeycombing the cliff. They are weakening its base and its body, and so the upper crust on which the fort was built, and into which its foundations were dug, is slipping away. If we imagine for a moment that nothing was done to save the fort or protect the cliff, but that all was left to nature to deal with, it would not be hard to picture what would happen. The cliff would gradually be eaten away: its gravel and clay would be drawn into the sea, and the Isle of Wight would become a little smaller. The same thing is going on at a good many places along the coast of the British Isles, as well as on the coast of Florida and in the Gulf of California in America.

The little islet of Heligoland in the North Sea, which once belonged to Great Britain, but was some years ago handed over to Germany, is so fiercely attacked by the sea in this way, that it almost has to be armour-plated in order to preserve its integrity. It is fenced in stone in order to protect it. What is happening on the coasts of islands like England and Heligoland is happening all over the world. It has always happened. If it had not happened in past ages there would be no British Isles at all, because once England and Scotland and Ireland were joined to Europe, and it would have been possible to walk across the North Sea from Harwich to the Hook of Holland. The North Sea was once dry land. But the sea encroached on it from the north, and the Atlantic Ocean battered a way through on the south, till the English Channel was bored through into the shallow waters of the newly-formed North Sea, and the lands that had once been part of Europe became these "sceptred isles set in the silver sea."

This is not all the story. What the sea takes away it gives again. Sir Thomas Holditch is our authority for saying that on some parts of the Pacific coast of America you may at some points see on the one hand dry land which by the shells found on it shows that the sea once flowed over it; while side by side with this raised land you may sail a boat over forests now sunk beneath the sea. The loss of bits and corners of England is serious--so serious that a Royal Commission on Sea Erosion, as the process is called, was appointed to inquire into the extent of the loss and the means by which it might be remedied. But in some parts of our coast the land is not losing, but gaining. If the sea takes away sand and gravel, chalk and shale and clay from the cliffs, these materials are not lost. Something is done with them. They must at some points, where the tides and currents of the sea deposit them, make the sea more shallow. Perhaps the sea lays them down as beds or sand-banks. Perhaps it carries them round the coast to some other point and there drops them. Can you not see that in this way the sea which at one point is dragging down the coast may at other points be building it up, or may be even constructing breakwaters made out of these stolen materials?

The sea is not the only carrier which is thus laying down beds of material. The rivers are doing the same thing. Every shower of rain washes some dirt--by which we mean sand or gravel or loam or chalk--from the land into the nearest rivulet. The rivulet hurries with it down to the neighbouring river, and the river carries it down to the sea. If the river is going very fast it carries most of its dirt along with it, and we generally find the river muddy after rain. But when the river slackens its pace, as it usually does when it nears the sea and meets the sea's tides, then it lets the dirt fall; and thus at the river's mouth we find mud-banks or sand-banks. If a river is left long enough to its own devices, these sand-banks will so increase in bulk that the mouth of the river will become shallower and shallower and will spread. It silts up, and when a river is needed for the navigation of ships large sums of money have to be spent, as in the Scheldt or at the mouth of the Thames, in dredging this mud so as to keep the channels clear.

Anybody who has ever visited the coast of these islands has become aware that the outline of the land is continually changing. On some parts of the east coast of England, as between Harwich and Walton-on-the-Naze, the sea appears to be slowly encroaching upon the land; fields where cattle grazed twenty or thirty years ago are now covered by the sea at high tide, and at low tide they are mere sandy wastes threaded by rivulets of sea-water. On the south coast of the Isle of Wight, between Sandown and the Culver Cliff (which is the most easterly point of the island), the land is being lost in another way. Some years ago a fort stood rather near the edge of the cliff, and a man might then have climbed round its seaward wall. He could not do so now. The outer sea-wall of the fort slipped into the sea long ago, and some of the inner fortifications have followed it; and the whole fort has had to be dismantled, lest even the inner landward wall should go the same way and slide with the solid ground down the cliff. The cause is easy to see. The wind and the waves are undermining and honeycombing the cliff, weakening its base and its body, and the upper crust on which the fort was built, and into which its foundations were dug, is slipping away for want of support. Let us suppose for a moment that nothing were done to save the fort or to protect the cliff, and that the whole matter were left to nature. We should have no difficulty in picturing the result. The cliff would gradually be eaten away; its gravel and clay would be drawn down into the sea; and the Isle of Wight would become a little smaller. The same thing is going on at a good many places along the coast of the British Isles, and it is going on as well on the coast of Florida and in the Gulf of California.

The little islet of Heligoland, in the North Sea, belonged at one time to Great Britain, and was handed over to Germany some years ago. The sea attacks it so fiercely that it almost has to be armour-plated to keep it whole, and it is in fact fenced in with stone for its protection. What the sea is doing to the coasts of England and of Heligoland it is doing all over the world, and it has always done it. Had it not done so in past ages there would be no British Isles at all; for England and Scotland and Ireland were once joined to Europe, and a man might then have walked dry-shod across the North Sea from Harwich to the Hook of Holland. The North Sea was once dry land. The sea encroached upon it from the north; the Atlantic battered a way through on the south, until the English Channel was bored through into the shallow waters of the newly-formed North Sea; and the lands that had once been part of Europe became these "sceptred isles set in the silver sea."

This is only half of the story, for what the sea takes away in one place it gives back in another. Sir Thomas Holditch is our authority for the statement that on parts of the Pacific coast of America you may see, on the one hand, dry land which the shells lying upon it show to have been once covered by the sea; while side by side with this raised land you may sail a boat over forests that have sunk beneath the water. The sand and gravel, the chalk and shale and clay, which the sea removes from the cliffs are not lost; they are laid down wherever the tides and currents happen to drop them, and there they make the sea shallower. The sea may spread them out as beds or heap them into sand-banks; or it may carry them round the coast to some other point and leave them there. Can you not see, then, that the same sea which is dragging down the coast at one point may be building it up at another? It may even be constructing breakwaters out of the very materials it has stolen.

The sea is not the only carrier that lays down beds of material in this fashion; the rivers are doing the same. Every shower of rain washes some dirt (by which we mean sand or gravel or loam or chalk) from the land into the nearest rivulet. The rivulet hurries with it down to the neighbouring river, and the river carries it down to the sea. If the river is running fast it bears most of its dirt along with it, and that is why we generally find a river muddy after rain. Changes in the outline of the land are continually taking place on the coast of these islands, and every one who has visited that coast has become aware of them. Between Harwich and Walton-on-the-Naze, on the east coast of England, the sea appears to be slowly encroaching on the land. Places which were grazing-fields twenty or thirty years ago are now covered by the sea at high tide; at low tide they are mere sandy wastes, threaded by rivulets of sea-water. On the south coast of the Isle of Wight, between Sandown and the Culver Cliff, which is the most easterly point of the island, the same loss of land is going on in another way. Some years ago a fort stood rather near the edge of the cliff there, and it was possible to climb round its seaward wall. That can no longer be done. The outer sea-wall of the fort slipped into the sea long ago, and some of the inner fortifications have followed it; and the whole fort has had to be dismantled, lest even the inner landward wall should slip with the solid ground down the cliff. It is easy to see what is happening here. The wind and the waves are undermining and honeycombing the cliff, weakening its base and its body, so that the upper crust on which the fort was built, and into which its foundations were dug, is slipping away. Let us suppose for a moment that nothing were done to protect the cliff, and that all were left to nature. It is not hard to picture the result. The cliff would gradually be eaten away; its gravel and clay would be drawn into the sea; and the Isle of Wight would become a little smaller. The same thing is going on at a good many places along the coast of the British Isles, as well as on the coast of Florida and in the Gulf of California.

The little islet of Heligoland, in the North Sea, once belonged to Great Britain, and some years ago was handed over to Germany. The sea attacks it so fiercely that it almost has to be armour-plated to preserve its integrity, and it is fenced in stone for its protection. What happens on the coasts of England and of Heligoland happens all over the world, and it has always happened. If it had not happened in past ages there would be no British Isles at all. England and Scotland and Ireland were once joined to Europe, and a man might then have walked across the North Sea from Harwich to the Hook of Holland, for the North Sea was dry land. The sea encroached on that land from the north; the Atlantic Ocean battered a way through from the south, until the English Channel was bored through into the shallow waters of the newly-formed North Sea; and the lands which had been part of Europe became these "sceptred isles set in the silver sea."

That is only half the story. What the sea takes away it gives again. On the authority of Sir Thomas Holditch, there are points on the Pacific coast of America where you may see, on the one hand, dry land which the sea once flowed over, as the shells found on it show; while side by side with this raised land you may sail a boat over forests now sunk beneath the sea. The loss of bits and corners of England is serious enough. Indeed, a Royal Commission on Sea Erosion (for so the process is called) was appointed to inquire into the extent of the loss and the means by which it might be remedied. Yet on some parts of our coast the land is gaining. The sand and gravel, chalk and shale and clay which the sea takes from the cliffs are not lost; something is done with them. Wherever the tides and currents of the sea deposit them, they must make the sea shallower. Perhaps the sea lays them down as beds or sand-banks; perhaps it carries them round the coast to some other point and drops them there. Can you not see that the sea which at one point is dragging down the coast may at another be building it up, or even constructing breakwaters out of these stolen materials? It can do both, and the beds it lays down are the proof.

The sea has a partner in this carrying trade, for the rivers also lay down beds of material. Every shower of rain washes some dirt (by which we mean sand or gravel or loam or chalk) from the land into the nearest rivulet. The rivulet hurries with it down to the neighbouring river, and the river carries it down to the sea. A river going very fast carries most of its dirt along with it, which is why we generally find a river muddy after rain. As it nears the sea and meets the sea's tides, however, the river usually slackens its pace; and when it slackens, it lets the dirt fall, so that at the river's mouth we find mud-banks or sand-banks. If a river is left long enough to its own devices, these banks will so increase in bulk that its mouth becomes shallower and shallower and spreads. The river silts up. Where a river is needed for the navigation of ships, large sums of money have to be spent in dredging the mud, as in the Scheldt or at the mouth of the Thames, so as to keep the channels clear.
